limitations: One control and one instrumented clean build per backend on a shared node; no statistical-significance claim.
A CPU sample or accumulated wait is not a removable wall-clock cost.
Wall occupancy describes whether any observed build thread could run; it does not reconstruct all within-compiler dependencies.
request_wait_answer identifies direct synchronous FUSE sleeps; other FUSE/page-cache paths may be classified by syscall or unresolved.
FUSE request lifetime includes queuing and service; dispatch and individual SL7 lock waits are not separated.
Runqueue delay combines scheduling competition and quota effects; cgroup throttling counters are separate and overlap.
Missing wakeup races are explicitly unresolved; CPU accounting is cross-checked against process totals.
Private package names, paths, invocation logs and raw traces are excluded from this report.

conclusions: The 189.92s SL7 profile is mostly concurrent compiler activity, but global activity hides dependency-local filesystem stalls. Its selected completion-chain units show 20.28s with no runnable thread in that unit and a direct FUSE wait present. The aws-lc-sys build-script alone shows 12.39s in that state. Basic LOOKUP plus GETATTR requests total only 7.02 overlapping request-seconds, versus 32.33 for WRITE, 12.99 for READ and 8.59 for OPENDIR. The next focused investigation should correlate those request tails with daemon queueing, backing-file I/O, publication and kernel CPU on the affected dependency chain. No new optimization was made. The noisy controls prevent claiming that any measured category explains a precise number of seconds of native-to-SL7 slowdown, or that all observed FUSE stalls are recoverable.
